analysis.one_liner: Taxes sugary drinks a penny per teaspoon of sweetener to fund diabetes and obesity programs.
analysis.headline: The SWEET Act, a one-cent-per-teaspoon soda tax to fund diabetes and obesity programs, was introduced in July 2014 with 7 sponsors, referred to two committees, and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a small federal tax on soda, energy drinks, sweet teas, and sports drinks — one cent for every 4.2 grams (about a teaspoon) of added sugar or corn syrup in the drink. The makers of these drinks would pay the tax. All the money would go to the federal Prevention and Public Health Fund and could be spent only on programs and research to fight diabetes, obesity, tooth decay, and other diet-related diseases, with a focus on the low-income communities and communities of color hit hardest. The idea is to nudge people toward cheaper, healthier drinks while creating a steady pot of money to treat and prevent the diseases sugary drinks are linked to.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people would gain on two fronts: a modest price signal steering them away from drinks linked to obesity and diabetes, and dedicated funding for prevention, treatment, and research programs aimed at the low-income communities and communities of color that bear the heaviest burden of diet-related disease. Public health programs and researchers would gain a new, protected revenue stream; Medicare and Medicaid budgets would benefit indirectly if prevention reduces long-term costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income communities facing diabetes and obesity

how_it_helps.text: It puts a small price penalty on sugary drinks — one cent per 4.2 grams (about a teaspoon) of caloric sweetener — designed to discourage the heavy consumption that the bill's findings link to obesity, type 2 diabetes, and tooth decay [S2][S3].

Every dollar raised goes to the Prevention and Public Health Fund and can be spent only on programs and research to reduce the human and economic costs of diabetes, obesity, dental caries, and other diet-related conditions in priority populations [S3].

The bill's findings note that obesity already costs an estimated $190 billion a year in medical spending, more than a fifth of it paid publicly through Medicare and Medicaid — costs the tax revenue would help offset by funding prevention [S3].
The one-cent rate rises with inflation after 2015, so the tax does not quietly shrink over time [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, producers, and importers of sugary drinks would pay the tax directly and would be expected to pass much of it to consumers through higher prices, so households that buy soda, energy drinks, or sweetened teas — disproportionately lower-income households — would bear much of the cost at the register.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sugary drink makers and their customers

drawbacks.text: Excise taxes on sugary drinks are regressive: low-income households buy more sugar-sweetened beverages than higher-income ones, so they would bear more of the tax, even though the bill's own findings show low-income people and communities of color bear the largest share of obesity and diabetes costs [S3].

The tax is levied on manufacturers, producers, and importers, who would be expected to pass at least part of it to consumers through higher shelf prices — meaning the cost lands on shoppers, not only on industry [S3].

The bill exempts drinks whose primary ingredient is milk or plant-based milk substitutes and 100% fruit or vegetable juices, and it does not tax artificially sweetened diet drinks, so some high-calorie or heavily marketed products would escape the tax entirely [S3].

Dedicating revenue to the Prevention and Public Health Fund locks the money to a narrow set of programs and populations, which supporters see as a guarantee and critics see as Congress micromanaging how health dollars can be spent [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is two-sided: a modest price signal that nudges people away from drinks with little nutritional value, plus a guaranteed funding stream for diabetes, obesity, and dental health programs aimed at the communities hit hardest. The main cost is regressivity — because low-income households buy more sugary drinks, they would pay more of the tax than wealthier households, even though they also bear the largest share of the diet-related disease burden the bill targets. Whether the tax helps or hurts a given household depends on whether it switches to cheaper untapped drinks (water, milk, 100% juice) or keeps paying. The industry-passed structure also means consumers may see only part of the price signal if companies absorb the tax. As a design, it is defensible but not perfect; the dedicated fund is the strongest part, the regressivity the weakest.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees on the day it was introduced, sent to a Health subcommittee two days later, and never came up for a hearing or a vote before the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 30, 2014, with about four months left in the two-year Congress [S5].

On the day of introduction it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee (which handles taxes) and the Energy and Commerce Committee, with the Speaker to decide which provisions each would consider [S5].
On August 1, 2014, it was referred to the Health Subcommittee — a step that typically precedes, but does not guarantee, a hearing [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugary drink makers and their suppliers, who keep selling an untaxed product, and the committee chairs whose inaction ended the bill. Ordinary people gained nothing: the prevention programs and the price signal never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sugary drink makers; the tax never arrived

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote its findings linking sugary drinks to obesity, diabetes, and tooth decay, with all revenue dedicated to prevention programs [S1][S3][S4].

for.name: 6 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill a total of seven sponsors but no Republican support [S4].

for.name: Rep. Jim Moran and Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.role: Original cosponsors who joined the introduction
for.what_they_did: Joined DeLauro in introducing the bill on July 30, 2014 [S3].

against.name: Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee with jurisdiction over the tax, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it dead after referral.

against.name: Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Co-chair of the second committee of referral; also took no action to move the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill sat in committees led by Republicans until the Congress ended.

industries.note: The bill taxes them one cent per 4.2 grams of caloric sweetener on every sale, raising the cost of the core product lines of companies like soda, energy drink, and sports drink makers. Their interest in blocking the tax ran against the bill's public health goal.

industries.industry: High-fructose corn syrup and sugar refiners
industries.note: The tax is defined per gram of caloric sweetener, including high-fructose corn syrup, so every additional teaspoon of sweetener sold into beverages carries a new cost, hitting corn refiners and sugar suppliers upstream.

industries.industry: Public health programs and research institutions
industries.note: The bill routes all tax revenue into the Prevention and Public Health Fund for diabetes, obesity, and dental programs in priority populations, creating a new dedicated funding stream. Its interest runs alongside the public's.
